utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please call the case -- Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. So today is July 10, 2007. I'd like to say hello to everyone, the Prosecution, Defence, the accused, and everyone in this courtroom. First, let me give to the floor to the registrar for a few IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness BD. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 625 under seal; the list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 626 under seal; the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 627; finally, the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 628 under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We need to go into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Open session. So for the next witness the Chamber has noted that the Prosecution needs two hours and 30 minutes. Defence thus will be granted, for 1D, 3D, and 4D, 35 minutes each unless they decide to split the time otherwise among themselves. 2D will be granted -- 2D, 5D, and 6D will be granted an hour each. Altogether, Defence will thus have four hours and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It was 3 hours and 30 minutes for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're supposed to finish by 4.25. So if you have objections, please limit them to the minimum to make sure that we really focus on the case rather than on objections that tend to waste time. Let's now introduce the witness. Prosecution, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness enters the courtroom, just a few very preliminary matters. I'd first like to introduce the Trial Chamber to Ms. Fridolijn Kuipers. She's present for the first time in the courtroom with us and she's been assisting with this witness. Secondly, in order to hopefully speed things along later this is the matter of one exhibit that I'd like to raise with the Trial Chamber now, hopefully it will make things go faster later and with the assistance of the greffier, the registrar, perhaps I could forward this document to the Trial Chamber so that it could look at the document while I speak about it. Mr. President, this is the original note, the original piece of paper that the witness will testify about during the course of his direct 10 July 2007 examination. It's marked as Exhibit P 2744. On the copies that are actually in e-court and which have been distributed, we have sort of a technical problem because based on the age of this document now five typewritten names which originally appeared on it and which can be noted, but they have faded, and so those names don't appear on the copy. I think that on real close examination with bifocals or a magnifying glass the names can be seen, but in any event, five names which appear on the document that we all have in front of us, don't appear at all because it's faded too much to copy any more. And I've raised this with a number of Defence counsel before the proceeding just to alert them to it. Several have indicated they don't see it as a problem. One has indicated that it could be a problem, and I don't know really at this point how we propose going forward. I can add: The names that are involved here are not the names of any of the accused. It's not something that's so direct as that. It is the name of alleged perpetrators of forced evictions. And so I am in the Trial Chamber's hands, I think, on how to proceed with this. We can wait until we get to that point in the direct and see how it develops, but in any event I wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to that now that the exhibit we're all looking at won't have the five names that appear on the original document because they've faded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Before giving the floor to Mr. Kovacic, the Chamber notes the following: We have a document. It's a white piece of paper with a couple of -- with eight red stripes on it, happened written in English are the following words: List of HVO soldiers who expelled Muslims on June 13, 1993, around 5.30 p.m. On the left-hand side of this document, there's the word "Dum", and typewritten right under this word is something that is very difficult to see but upon scrutiny you can decipher the names Martinovic Vinko; Ernest Takac; Peco Nino-Ziga; Bobo Peric; and Damir Peric. And in handwriting as number 6 Viktor Markovic is added in the same ink as the ink used to write "List of HVO soldiers." That's the document. There are five names that have been typed on this paper. Martinovic Vinko, Ernest Takac, Peco Nino-Ziga, Bobo Peric and Damir Peric. This is what the Chamber can say about this original document. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in a preliminary conversation with my learned friend, I said that I would object as a matter of principle without going into the issue of the relevance or irrelevance of this document, especially for General Praljak. I have to say that this is a purely forensic issue. As Your Honour yourself has just said, part of the text has completely faded and I was unable to read it. Your Honour seems to have sharper eyesight than me. Another part is less faded. I think as forensic science stands today a laboratory would not have a problem with this. We have two different parts of the document. One has faded and the other not, so we don't not know whether the entire document was composed at the same time or whether something was added on later. Secondly, the OTP has broken some sacrosanct rules of legal procedure which exist in all countries whether rich or poor, developed or undeveloped, and this is the second incident where the OTP has allowed a piece of evidence to deteriorate. If Your Honours recall, we recently had a videotape which was unusable after a lapse of time because it had not been properly kept. I don't know whether the OTP will come up with another exhibit sooner or later which will be important for my case which will need to be handled forensically because it was not properly stored, and for that reason I object as a matter of principle to the use of such exhibits without previous forensic analysis, and I wish to point out that the OTP has allowed a piece of evidence to deteriorate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm discovering this right now. Where does it come from? Who handed this document in? Which archive does it come from? Could you give us the brief history of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The witness will testify that the document was handed to him while he was on patrol in Mostar during May of 1993, which is the period of time that he'll be testifying about. It was -- there's a notation on it which actually is the very bottom right hand where it says attachment PB. PB stands for Plony Bos. That's the name of the OTP investigator who interviewed the witness and took this and other things that he provided during his interview on, I believe, the 13th of August, 2001, with the witness's initials and Ms. Bos's initials next. So since that time the document's been in the custody of the OTP evidence unit in the vault. And I had to sign it out in order to get it into the courtroom to provide this clarification. May I suggest, Mr. President, that perhaps we proceed with the witness. The Trial Chamber can hear his story about it and assess the authenticity and the probative value of the document at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you right, in a street in Mostar that some person handed this document to the witness, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The typewritten part was given to the witness. The handwriting on the right which you read, Mr. President, list of HVO soldiers who expelled people, that is the handwriting of the witness, which he made at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So if I understood right, in the street, he was handed this document where five names were typewritten, and he added by hand "List," and added Viktor Markovic as number 6. That's what happened. At least that's what we understood. I guess the best is to go into the in-chief and we'll find out with the witness. Now, let's bring the witness into the courtroom. I can give you the document back but maybe you also need to circulate it with the counsel of Defence. They can look at it and Mr. Praljak can also look at it - does he need glasses to look at it? - and so we'll circulate the document first and then we'll get it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor gave us an opportunity to look at the document before the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being brought in, could I remind the technical people. Excuse me. The witness was an ECMM monitor, European Commission Monitoring Mission. He's going to be talking and testifying about numerous reports that he made as an ECMM monitor; reports were provided to us confidentially. We will not need to go into private session when he testifies about those. However, the arrangement, as with earlier ECMM witnesses, is that the reports themselves will not be shown publicly on the monitors outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please tell me your name, surname and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Antoon Willem Maria Van der Grinten, born 11 November, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your job now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a professional officer in the Royal Netherlands Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you tell us what your rank is in the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My rank is lieutenant-colonel. I'm infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you already testified in court regarding facts that happened in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you're testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the second time, sir, Your Honour. I did it in January 2002 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In January 2002. But in which case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case against Tuta and Stela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you Prosecution witness or Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prosecution witness, sir. 10 July 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please now take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is a correction in the transcript on page 11, line 6. The witness has given, all in all, three first names, Antoon, Willem, and Maria and the second and third have not been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have three surnames, Antoon Willem Maria; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. Let me explain how the hearing is going to be organised. You have already testified so this will come as no surprise to you. First, you will answer questions put to you by Mr. Stringer. I'm sure you already met him during the proofing session. Prosecution will ask questions and will present documents at the same time, and you will be asked to comment on these documents. After this phase, Defence counsel on your left or maybe even the accused will cross-examine you and will thus ask you questions. Four Judges on the Bench can interrupt at any time to put questions to you, but as far as possible we would rather not intervene and only take the floor after questions have been put by either Prosecution and Defence, but sometimes we step in because of the document, and we would rather just ask questions immediately about a document that's presented on the screen. Please try and focus on your answers and be very concise. If you do not understand a question, just ask for a reformulation of the question. There will be breaks every hour and a half. These are 20-minute breaks. And this hearing will end tomorrow at 4.25, but first we'll -- today we'll stop at 7.00. Of course it's not going to go on forever until tomorrow. So tonight we will stop at 7.00 p.m., resume tomorrow at 2.15, and we'll stop at 4.25. Now, without further ado I will now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Van der Grinten. Welcome. Before I start asking you about the relevant time period, let me just ask you some questions about your background. Have you been a member of the Netherlands royal army since 1971?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did you attend the Royal Military Academy for the Netherlands from 1971 to 1975?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In 1979 and 1980 did you serve on behalf of the Dutch -- royal Dutch army in the United Nations mission in Lebanon?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes, in UNIFIL.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in 1986 and 1987 did you again serve as a member of the royal Dutch army, the United Nations mission in Lebanon, subsequently Syria and Israel?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In 1993, were you then assigned, again, as a representative of the Royal Dutch Army, to join the ECMM, the European Community Monitoring Mission, then in Hungary?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That was my first station; correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How long did you stay with ECMM in Hungary?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I stayed there almost four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then after just four weeks were you asked or transferred then to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I was transferred then in weekends to Mostar, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll come back to that period of time obviously. Couple things then, your experience after having gone into the Mostar region. From August 2000 to October of 2004 did you work as a lieutenant-colonel in the Royal Netherlands Army as chief of the operations branch at the NATO subregional headquarters in Izmir, Turkey?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And from October 2004 to the present, have you been based in Madrid with NATO as chief of land operations for the NATO subregion -- southern subregion, I should say?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes, from November 2004 actually up to now. That is my position now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in that capacity are you responsible for all NATO operations in its southern region?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Monitoring.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, going back then to the relevant period for our purposes, May of 1993, you say you arrived in Mostar as an ECMM monitor. Do you recall roughly the date or the period in the month of May when you actually arrived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think it was the 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you travel to Mostar I guess from Hungary via Zagreb and then through Split into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We travelled first to the headquarters in Zagreb to be briefed about the situation and to get more instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to clarify, I have said -- I have mentioned Mostar, but in fact when you were then based in the Mostar region, where were your offices located, the ECMM office that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: They just moved, actually, the coordination centre out of -- out of Mostar. In the previous time they had a centre in downtown Mostar, but they moved it to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you -- recognising that you weren't there at the time, did you know or did you learn why the office was moved out of Mostar to Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That had all to do with the security; a secure environment was not longer there at the place where they had it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the office was moved for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has heard the testimony of other individuals who worked with the ECMM in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I'm not going to ask you very much about the overall mandate of ECMM in the country, but I will ask you a couple questions about the structure as it pertained to you -- as it pertained to you in Mostar. You mentioned already a coordination centre. Could you tell us what the coordination centre was?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: In the ECMM organisation, the coordination centre was actually the lowest level where the work was done for Zagreb in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. How many coordination centres were located in the region of Western Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: It's hard to recall, but at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask it this way: You say you were with the coordination centre located in Mostar but actually based in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was -- we'll see it in the reports. Was your coordination centre called M2 or Mike 2 in terms of the organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No. The coordination centre was called Mostar, but it consisted out of three teams at that time. Three teams to cover not only Mostar but a region bigger than Mostar, but the teams had their base in Siroki Brijeg and came -- at least two teams came daily back, and the third team every week at least once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was there a team called M1 that covered Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then your team, M2, covering Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was there another team called M3 that was covering the Medjugorje area south of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then I don't think we'll see any reports, but was there subsequently an M4 that was added for Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, but that happened in August. So at the end of my period, my time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just to set the time frame, then, were you then working as a part of the M2 team for Mostar from this period, late May until the late part of August when you left?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So roughly three months.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, above the coordination centre level what was the next highest office or -- or centre that you reported to from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We reported to the regional centre in Zenica what was meant by a diplomat. He had more -- more coordination centres, of course, and all the reports he received on daily base were then summarised and sent to Zagreb, to the main headquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So Zagreb, then, was the main ECMM headquarters for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, recognising that you were working on the local level in Mostar, can you give the Trial Chamber just a brief idea of the tasks and the mandate that you had as ECMM monitors in Mostar during that three-month period?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: The main task was to provide around-the-clock, seven days a week a picture what was going on in the region in, let's say our area of responsibility, and for the M2 team that was downtown and the direct vicinities, the outskirts of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just in general, how did you work? How did you go about trying to find the information, make the picture to report about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- we established, let's say, a kind of network by NGOs, IOs, officials, but also people in the street to get as much as possible information and verify that kind of information by various sources. That was the most important thing to -- to give the right picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, based on the information that you obtained from various sources, did you make reports?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- we sent our reports -- we made a report every day when we returned to our home base, and that was before darkness, discussed the outcome of the work we did over the last period and then summarised it, gave an assessment according to a fixed format, and that was then before sent to Zenica approved by the head of the coordination centre. That was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who was the head, then, of the coordination centre that was for Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: When I arrived, the head of the centre was a retired full German colonel. His name was Klaus Nissen, and he was replaced in July by a just-retired three-star British general, Sir Martin Garrod.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've been saying "we," and I should ask, your team, the M2 team, was it a two-man team, and if you could just tell the Trial Chamber who your partner was?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry. I forgot to explain you the team. It was a fixed team of two members and driver, but the driver came from the driver pool, actually. The other member was a major of the Spanish Army, Jesus Amatriain, and I worked with him during the -- during the whole time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Amatriain, what country was he from?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Spain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you and your colleague Mr. Amatriain then collaborated in preparing these reports that were then sent to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me then direct you to the binder, Colonel, that's in front of you and ask you to look at Exhibit P 2496. And recognising that the date of this may be just before your arrival, I want to ask you first, do you recognise this? Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, this document was a daily summary by the predecessors. In this case it is signed by Milverton, who was a British officer. We relieved him, actually, in the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Because the -- the memo makes reference to a couple things I'm going to be asking you about, and the first is the joint commission meeting right there on the first page, and I wanted to ask you whether you then became familiar and involved in the process of joint commissions that's referred to here.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That joint commission was established after the Vance-Owen agreement, and that already was in place. So we replaced actually Milverton and his colleague at that moment. By the way, Jesus Amatriain was there already. He arrived a little bit early or so. I jumped in, actually, as the new member.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: And we were briefed about this in the week when we took over the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: The purpose of the joint commission was actually to get the -- the -- all the parties around the table and to discuss -- to implement, actually, that what was feasible in the Mostar area on the ground according to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. And you said the parties. Just for the record, we're talking about the HVO on the one side and the armija on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: In this case, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned Vance-Owen, then, and there's reference to that here and in other reports as well. Your approach to Vance-Owen, was it on the local level or was it coming from a higher level?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: It was translated, let's say, from the local level to the work we were doing in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: With the ultimate goal of the joint commission being?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Two: To establish a discussion and to finally apply to what was mentioned in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In general was the joint commission something that was intended to accomplish certain goals, get the parties to work together on certain things?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely to stop the -- the hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit for you would be the next one in the binder, which is marked 2550. Can you turn to that? Colonel, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I do, because my handwriting is on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The typewritten part, first of all, do you recall who you -- well, did you receive this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And from whom? It says "Tertio" at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes, Tertio stands for M3, so it's going from our team, M3, located or working in the Medjugorje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then over the right-hand side there is the handwritten "28 May, 1993." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that the date that you received this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That is the date that we received it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, what this says is that -- I won't read the whole thing, that that there is a plan for today for our tomorrow morning or for tomorrow morning "to arrest all the male persons (Mike of course) from the settlements which are on the first front line." And it continues making references to various locations, streets, and the Heliodrom. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that -- your interpretation of that message, what's -- what are you being told there in this note?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may for a second. Can we lay a foundation? Who exactly did this note come from? We have something down there on the bottom but on what basis? Was this on the basis of investigation, tips, some unknown confidential informant, because now he's being asked to translate what somebody else has written.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you heard the objection. Would you like to address that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. May have a ruling, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm covering to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, if I don't say anything, it means that I agree. So let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I recognise it. It is part of the report of the M3 team, because we discussed our reports at the end of the day, and it makes clear because -- because Mike, of course, stands for -- Mike is -- is -- is the NATO abbreviation of -- of the M, and that stands here for Muslim. So that clarifies where it is all about, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I mean, we'll talk more about sources later, but did you in M2, did you communicate with your colleagues in M3 and elsewhere and share information?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We did. This is an example of that at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the handwriting farther down relates to a hundred confirmed cases, occupation of houses, apartments by HVO. Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what it is that caused you to make that notation there or how you -- why you indicated a confirmation?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, it fits probably with messages and information we got from the Mostar area, because our reports normally were based on confirmed information and not about rumours. I mean, when you -- when you read in one of our reports rumour, then it was a rumour and not confirmed. All the other information were real statements or at least confirmed by one or more sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit is P 2564. 2564.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Colonel, the document that we see signed Tertio, you said it was M3. When I see the text, I get the feeling that M3 is speaking about a possible plan that would be executed on the same day or the next day aiming to arrest certain people who were Muslims. So I assume that M3 would have had this information from a source, either the HVO or the ABiH, but the source is not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's correct, Your Honour. And -- and I'm very sorry that I don't answer that question, because it came from the team, and after 14 years probably it's hard to give an answer upon this, where it originally came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But when you have this type of information, do you not look into or do you not submit it to -- or submit to Zenica, to your superiors, that there may be a large-scale operation that is going to be launched in order to alert everyone? Was this information passed on to your superiors in the chain of command or in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, definitely, because this only shows that we were exchange -- that we exchanged information on our level, and this definitely is in the summary of the head of the coordination centre sends to Zenica, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- I hope to link this up or at least connect it with some of the exhibits to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on that subject about then reporting such information up your reporting chain, I think it's useful now to look at this next exhibit, P 2564. 2564. I think you're going to have to skip one to get to it.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't recognise this document because it don't come from -- from our CC. This comes from Zagreb. That means from -- from the Danish delegation. So it is on a higher level. Two levels just in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So this is just a document from the headquarters of ECMM based in Zagreb. Are you able to recognise it as that? I'm not asking you if you saw it before but whether it appears to be an ECMM document from Zagreb headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's definitely from the Danish delegation within the headquarters in Zagreb, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time was it -- Denmark had the EC Presidency and so --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah. So they finalised the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to continue with that, the information contained in these reports, then, coming from the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb, do you know, and if you don't, that's fine, do you know where these reports then were destined? Who were the ultimate recipients of the information contained in these reports?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, you can see that. At the end of the document you see the distribution list, and that shows clearly that this went, of course, back to the heads of the regional centres, to the heads of the coordination centres, and to a lot of -- a number of liaison officers in the various regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: And internal -- internal means within the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I then direct you, if you look at the top right-hand corner, to page 4 of 18. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is a section that relates to Mostar update brief of 25 May. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So this is actually dated right at the time of your arrival in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting back to the question that the President had, 10 July 2007, I want to direct your attention to then page 7 of 18 of this document. If you could turn three more pages. The very top paragraph states: "Monitors stated that Muslims were still being expelled from their homes in HVO-held districts of Mostar, and on the 20th May were sleeping in the streets around the armoured cars of SpaBat deployed in the city." Now, recognising that you weren't in Mostar on the 20th of May, is this then reflecting the information regarding the evictions that is in part indicated in the other note that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the information's flowing up the chain, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes. To answer the President's question, this is a good example where you see that the Mostar update is the information gathered by our CC and Zenica, and it comes from our teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Used by finally the Presidency, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so based on what you knew again, recognising that you're not in Zagreb, but if you know, was it then in Zagreb where analysis occurred and reports from various locations were put together to construct an overall picture?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Getting back to this issue of evictions in the Mostar area, let me direct you now to the next exhibit, which is P 2600. And I want to use this exhibit to introduce again the subject of evictions. Perhaps I could just ask you to look at these photographs and tell the Trial Chamber what -- what these are about.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: These pictures are quite familiar to me because I took them myself after we were tipped that some people were forced to move in the night before, and we went to that location and found this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Without mentioning any names, unless you wish to, could you give an indication of who the source of information was on this tip?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: At that time I think this was -- this was reported by our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did your interpreter -- was your interpreter a Muslim person living in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately the time frame in which these photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, you can see the date is on the picture. It is the 1st of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So again just to continue, you got a tip from your interpreter about this sort of thing happening, and then tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We went to the spot. The door -- we talked to the neighbours to verify what happened over there, and they opened the apartment and showed us what happened. And -- well, the most important thing is that the first message was actually by -- by a second source confirmed, and taking the photographs was probably for us a kind of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall roughly what part of Mostar this apartment 10 July 2007 was located?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Not that far, I remember, from the place where -- where our interpreter was living with her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is on the west side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, on the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, forgive me if you've already said this. The first -- the second -- the second photograph has -- could you describe that and particularly what part of the apartment that -- those markings were located?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That are bullet marks in the ceiling, because they told us that they were forced by HVO soldiers and were intimidated by -- by fire. So this finally was the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During this time or at any time did you also hear about the looting of property, that is, taking property out of Muslims apartments such as this?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. At that time we got various messages and information about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next exhibit is marked P 2622. And, Colonel, this is actually the first report that we've -- we've got now that is -- is originating from you and your colleague, Jesus Amatriain. And before we go into the specific parts of it, just so the Trial Chamber knows, I'd like you to briefly tell us the format of these, how these are organised, looking at the section with the numbers beginning "General situation." What was the way in which these reports were generally organised by you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you see the paragraphs, and the paragraphs were fixed starting with "General Situation", then "Cease-fire Violations". That was a directed subject from the peace agreement, of course. The same for paragraph 5, "Tripartite Meeting" was coming from the agreement as well. In fact, we were dealing with only two in Mostar at that moment. "Humanitarian aid", we always noted very carefully who we met and the results of -- of that meeting. Other subjects and administration was more about our own business, talking about logistics for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this particular report, first of all -- well, do you recognise this as one that you and your colleague Mr. Amatriain prepared and sent to the Zenica regional centre?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I recognise -- when you go to the top of the message you see "NL Burum", and then day time group and a series of numbers, and especially the date and the time. That means that it was sent -- this message, this is a copy from our transmitter, and this is a message sent by our satellite system. Burum stands for the satellite system. It means that this was sent to Zenica, info the four you see under ECMM restricted. And that happened every night after approval of the chief of the coordination centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you'd prepare your report jointly and then your chief would approve it, and then --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: And then it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. If you would turn the page, then, to page 2, because I'm not going to -- I just want to -- use this one to introduce another subject that we'll be talking about. Directing your attention to item number 8 which relates to the situation on the east side, "it's becoming critical." And then moving down there's a reference to pressure, "it would be a good idea to put more political pressure on the HVO in order to re-establish the supply of water and humanitarian aid to the BiH side." First of all, by this point, which is the 3rd of June, had you actually gone into East Mostar yourself to see the situation there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That needs maybe more clarification. Sorry. The way of -- the way of working was the following: We -- we made a list of points or people we wanted to see the day before, and we had to start, of course, on the west side because Siroki Brijeg is -- is located west of Mostar north-west more or less. And what we always did then only when it was not possible but let's say probably 90 per cent of the time that we went downtown we always visited the west bank, went to the east bank and back. So we always were visiting both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at this point in early June, was it in fact the situation on the east side becoming -- that it was becoming critical, as you indicate?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you indicate the HVO had some control over the water supply? Was that the case as you found it?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: At that time, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the same was true with respect to humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well, because that was a matter of a -- that -- the possibility to get humanitarian aid in was restricted by check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And one other point. You indicated in item 7 here meetings with persons who are associated with the 4th Corps of the ABiH. And I think I just want to ask you this now: To what extent did you accept things they told you about the situation versus going out on your own and trying to confirm the things that they were telling you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, in principle that was not different on the west or on the east bank. We noted what was stated by the people there or the commanders or the people in charge and then tried to verify that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit is P 2635. Are you able to recognise this as one of the M2 reports prepared by you and your colleague in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And the bottom of page 2 here there's a reference to Amigo Jesus and the Flying Dutchman. Would you be the Flying Dutchman as referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Looking at this there's a reference to your armoured vehicle having been shot at from the west bank. I wanted to ask you to briefly tell the Trial Chamber about that incident, and also comment on your statement in the report here that you guess it came from the direction of a sniper in the building belonging to the HVO, or in one building belonging to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. At that time, we are talking here about the 4th of July, we were still able to cross the Neretva --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt. You said 4th of July and I note the report is 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, sorry, sorry. I misread it. No, the 4th of June. Sorry. At that time we were still able to use the Tito Bridge in the centre to go from west to east just through the confrontation line with our armoured car, and that is what we did as long as it was possible. This reports -- this report clarifies that we were shoot when we were halfway the Tito Bridge from the east side, and by our knowledge at that moment and by the impact, I mean the knowledge, the military knowledge of this, because there was never a real investigation about this, but by our military knowledge the shot was direct fire by line of sight from higher ground. And from the position of the car and the angle of the impact, the only possibility here was what we called from the blue bank building, and that was a dominant building in the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You actually said that we were shot -- or "when we were halfway the Tito Bridge from the east side", and I want to clarify that. Which side did the -- the round, the shot, originate from to the best of your knowledge? Did it come from the west side or the east side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We went from the west to the east side. So the bullet -- we headed to the headquarters in the east side. So the bullet came from the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned this blue bank building and we'll come back to it. Is that what you believed or as you indicate here you guessed that the building or that the bullet came from?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were aware that there were armija positions on the west bank of the Neretva, so it was not possible to completely rule out which side actually fired the bullet?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Not by our knowledge at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibit P 2634. Actually, it's the previous exhibit. You'll have to go back one. Just to move things along, if I could ask is that a photograph of your ECMM vehicle, and does it indicate the hit from the bullet in the rear left-hand corner of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as indicated on the photograph, was this photo taken on the 4th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We took this photograph on the 4th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is - excuse me - 2661. Colonel, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. President. The quality of the image is not as nice as we would like, but it's the best we've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm start first of all with the bottom on the handwriting, Colonel, where it says Doc named and then the date of 7th of June, 1993, and then the letters -- or the numbers 01. Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is and whether you saw it before?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a document I handed over in January 2002. It is a document what we received from the commander of the BH army on the east side, at that time Colonel Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the date that you received this letter from him?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That is the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's -- so you wrote the date on there.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: And the 01 stands for the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you say you were present in East Mostar and he personally gave this to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That -- that happened various times, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, recognising that this is a protest letter from Colonel Pasalic, I want to just direct your attention to the middle of the page. He makes reference to the hospital not receiving any help, citizens not allowed to have a supply of water, and there is permanent expelling of citizens, exclusively Muslims, and all this is done in front of you. So this protest letter, those complaints about the hospital, the water and the expulsions, is this something that you found was happening based on your -- your presence and your contacts with various sources?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That is what we experienced at that time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you if you recall at roughly the same period of time your vehicle being the target of a -- of a hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That is another time that we were shot at, and to our -- to our belief also from the blue bank building, but -- but in western direction. So not from the blue bank building to the east as the first time what the picture showed of the car, but in this case we were on the west side at a location we used, a school on the west side, just at the border of the confrontation line. The school what we used in previous days for that joint committee. We were very familiar with the location there, and we went there to -- to make a sanitary stop, and suddenly when we were out of the car and into the building a grenade was fired and impacted just three metres from our car with our Italian driver inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was anyone injured in that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the same car the photo we've just looked at that had all the markings of the ECMM and the --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn now to Exhibit P 9615, which I believe is in your binder. If I can hand it -- it's a photograph which I can hand you. It may speed things along. The registrar can hand you a copy of that and may be something we can see on our television monitors as well.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've been talking about this blue bank building, and I want to ask if you recognise this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. This is what we called the blue bank building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In what part of Mostar was this located?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: It was on the west -- on west side of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it doesn't look very blue to me, so maybe you can explain why it's called --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry. You still see in the lower -- the lower floors you still see some -- some glass, blue glass pane impact, and that is why we called it the blue bank building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is this the location you referred to when you believed as being the -- the location where the sniper shot came from?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, we know that this building was used by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 2675.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, just a minute. I'm still on this photograph of this Blue Building. You said, "We knew that snipers used this building." You said this at line 7, page 36. What I am interested in is the following: At the time, I'd like to know who controlled this building. Were there HVO soldiers on the bottom floor, or could anyone just walk in, climb up, shoot, and then leave? According to what you saw at the time, could you tell us who controlled the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I strongly believed that HVO was controlling the snipers in the building at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but on the ground floor were there HVO soldiers that were posted to guard this building? You say, "I'm almost sure. I strongly believed that HVO was controlling the building," but was there a presence of HVO with soldiers stationed on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- we never got the impression that it was that -- that secured as you -- as you are -- are talking about. I mean, a control -- a fixed control that they had, a total grip they had on who went in or out, we never were able to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify that a little bit, Colonel. The building itself, which -- which zone was it located in, the HVO zone or the ABiH zone?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: The HVO-controlled zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. At this period of time was the confrontation line well established so that it was either one or the other, or was there the possibility that it could have been ABiH in that building?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No, not at that time, because the positions were fixed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The -- the next exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, have I -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 2675, Colonel, is the next exhibit. Is this one of the reports that you and your colleague made from 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, again, just coming back briefly to the joint commission. There's a reference at the bottom of this first page to the joint commission meeting having met for the first time on the east side. And then continuing, it says: "Both parts decided to call off the joint commission," and then the reasons are stated there. Were you present at this meeting of the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Based on your observations, how well was the joint commission working during this -- this admittedly short period of time that you had been in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, the results of the joint committee at that time were very poor. It was more showing willingness to sit around the table but no willingness to solve the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection -- there are references here to efforts to create a mixed civilian police force, and I just wanted to ask again briefly if you could tell us what that's about and how much success that was met with by the parties.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I know that it was a part of -- a part of the agreement to -- to set that up, and UNCIVPOL was dealing with that at that time to get regular policemen from the east and west bank working to the patrollings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And was ultimately accomplished?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P 2678. Now, Colonel, this is an ECMM report dated 8th of June, 1993. However, this appears to be originating from team M3. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you know the -- the M3 team members at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We met them every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just turning to the third page. Their names appear there, Koskie and Smulders.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes, Brad Koskie was a Canadian officer and Chris Smulders was Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, there is a reference to a meeting with Pero Markovic, the mayor of Capljina. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And recognising -- well, was Capljina within your area of responsibility on M2?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No, that was M3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: M3's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. My question about this document is found on the next page, about two-thirds of the way down. There is a reference to derogatory and prejudiced views about Muslims that were expressed by Pero Markovic. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. My question is simply whether in your own dealings with any HVO officials whether you encountered is similar views on part of HVO or HVO government persons.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, this statement is a statement we heard more by officials. Such a kind of statement I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. Could you elaborate on that or ... ?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, such a position as -- as stated here was something we heard often in -- in our conversations with officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. HVO officials?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: HVO officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just for the record, we're going to be talking about some of the meetings you had with some of the accused in this case, so were any of these sorts of views expressed by any of the accused who are in this case that we'll be talking about, Mr. Stojic, Pusic, Prlic, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Is there anyone in particular that you recall as whom you associate these sorts of comments with in your own dealings?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We were dealing -- we were dealing with the HVO LO during that time frame, named Stanko Maric, and he -- he was a man who -- who sometimes talked in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P 2703.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll go through it swiftly. If I could just very briefly touch on this one, I think I can finish it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Again, can you remember, is this one of the reports prepared by you and your colleague in Mostar, M2?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: 2703. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Right. This is a report of M2, our report, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And here it's dated the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The -- I want to introduce this subject just before the break and then we could come back to it. Item number 5 relates to a visit to the hospital on the west bank. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In order to hand over a letter from the armija, Colonel Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. At this time and throughout the remainder of your time there in Mostar, did you work on trying to arrange exchanges of doctors and medical supplies to both hospitals, one on the west and one on the east?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can leave it at that for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a break, a 20-minute break and we will resume at 4.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have the floor, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Colonel, just before the break we were looking at Exhibit 2703, and I had directed your attention to item number 5 regarding your visit to the hospital on the west bank, and you had stated that you spent time, maybe a lot of time, trying to organise the exchange of medicines and doctors as well, we'll talk about, between the hospital on the west side and the hospital on the east side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: As of this time, the 11th of June, 1993, could you give the Trial Chamber just an idea, a comparison in terms of the facilities that existed in the east side hospital in East Mostar versus the hospital in West Mostar? How did the two of them compare?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, at that time in West Mostar we were talking about a normal organised hospital with the full -- full equipped with specialists, a good organisation. On the east side, in the contrary, was -- we're talking about -- we called it a war hospital, or the war hospital, located on the east bank in a former school, and I remember that very well. Very bad conditions, very small place with a lot of patients. At that time, they brought in also dead bodies. They were operating in the kitchen, but more worse was that the team of doctors was a very small one, and they were working sometimes around the clock without any sleep. Also, they had at that time not all the medicines, medication or whatever, equipment, but also facilities to treat the people in the right way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So then you set about trying to arrange for supplies and doctors and medicines to go from west to east in order to improve the situation in the east side war hospital.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, because for instance the Red Cross or the UNHCR was not -- was not deployed any more downtown Mostar because it was too dangerous, so we took over. And we actually were the only ones who were able to cross on to visit the east bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So the only ones, the only international observers.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. In the same report, moving up, in item 3 there is reference to a meeting on that day with Bruno Stojic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Sorry, are you talking about 2703?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 2, item 3.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you first, a meeting with Bruno Stojic at that time. Tell us if you recall, who was Bruno Stojic? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic was Ministry of Defence. He had the office at the MOD of HVO, and we visit him frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I notice that in this particular report there's a reference to a meeting with him. However, there isn't any information about what, if anything, was said at the meeting, and can you comment on that or explain why that might be the case?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, normally, as I explained before, we made a list of subjects, asking questions in the hope to get an answer, but sometimes the answers were pending. And when there are no comments here, then probably nothing -- no answers and no valid issues were discussed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Nothing of substance?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then moving down to item 6 on the same page. This contains your assessment, that of you and your colleague, Mr. Amatriain. There's a comment there about HVO wanting to improve their situation in the area of Donja Mahala, as well as make impossible the life in the east bank. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is that your assessment as of that time, that the HVO was wanting to make life impossible on the east side, the east bank?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Improve their situation means here strangling the positions, but making the life impossible on the east side was at that time exactly what happened, yeah, according to our observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit, 2721, is from the very next day, the 11th of June, 1993. Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is this one of the reports that you and your colleague made from M2 regarding your activities on the 11th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this particular report, we'll walk through it first, first page at the bottom there's a reference to a meeting with Mr. Pusic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what was the position of Mr. Pusic at this time?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic at that time was the deputy military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is he also someone that you would meet with from time to time?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Where was his office located?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: His office was also located in the same building where we found the office of Mr. -- of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So they were located in the same building?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to page 2 there's a reference here about a third of the way down, reference to a visit to the Heliodrom prison, a discussion with the deputy director, and then farther down there's an assessment of your visit. Could you just briefly inform the Trial Chamber how that visit to the Heliodrom came out -- came about, how you gained entry, and what was the situation that you found at that Heliodrom when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. When we heard that at the Heliodrom a lot of prisoners were transported, and by the knowledge that the Red Cross was not working or not issue any more for the same reason I just mentioned, security reasons, we tried to get access to the Heliodrom prison and requested permission and approval from Mr. Pusic to go there and to visit the situation, to monitor the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And on that -- on that point, then, where did you go to gain your approval? What sort of approval or documentation were you provided?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: I think that we needed an official paper signed by him to -- to give us -- to provide us access to the commander with our questions we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then taking that paper from Mr. Pusic or his office, were you then able to get into the Heliodrom and to look around?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tell us about that. What happened when you arrived there, and what did you find?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, we went there and had first an introduction by at that time the chief of the Heliodrom prison. We asked him a lot of questions, actually, after he gave us, let's say, figures. It's all in this report by the way. After that we were able, I think after about an hour, to talk to the prisoners and to visit them. Not all, but a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the prisoners you spoke to, can you describe in general what was the conditions of their confinement? What sort of condition were they in?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: The condition was very poor because they didn't know why they were there. There were no -- there were -- let me -- let me use the right sequence, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: They were not accused. Most of them didn't know why they were there for actually and how long they should stay. So the overall impression was that they were gathered or transported over there without any justification. And by the way, the situation was -- was bad. I think that in this report it says that we saw a lot of people in very small rooms with some mattresses for HVO soldiers, and the rest was even not able to sleep in a decent way, no exercises or fresh air, that kind of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were those the things that they told you or that you saw when you were --

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: No, we saw it. We went into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, did you -- were you able to determine whether these prisoners or what -- what was the composition in terms of prisoner of war versus civilian?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Well, that's hard to recall now, but I want to stick then to the text in this report because that is what we finally noted and what definitely was correct for -- for the part we were able to -- to visit. That means there were HVO soldiers we saw, but most of them were civilians and in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were out at the Heliodrom, did you then have any discussions with any of the authorities on the HVO side?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yeah. By -- I remember that -- that -- let's say the overall comments of -- of the chief at that time was, "I can't answer you. You have to see the officials." And by "officials," of course he was mentioning Mr. Coric, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: So we planned to visit them and to ask them the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- I want to direct your attention - excuse me - to page 3 of that report just on that last point you raised, because it has been a long time. You wrote: "He told us that he does not know any of the reasons why people are in prison and that only Mr. Coric or Mr. Pusic know these reasons." Is that what you were then told? Is that an accurate reflection of what you were told by the deputy out at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, can you remember, is Exhibit 2731. It's a little bit of a different format from the other ones, but do you recognise this as one of your M2 ECMM reports dated 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it your handwriting at the bottom with the date written there?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There's a reference here to -- on this date, the 12th of June, a lieutenant of the Spanish Battalion, a platoon commander who was killed in the course of a convoy that was taking medicine to the east side hospital. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tell us what you can about your recollection of that incident.

utterances.speaker: ANTOON VAN DER GRINTEN
utterances.text: We arranged within the contacts between the west and -- the west bank hospital and the east war hospital, we arranged for the first time a transport of medicines by UNPROFOR. So UNPROFOR, the platoon -- a platoon for APCs picked up the medicines and equipment at the west bank and transported that to the east.
